newsitem.title: USA: Pakistan may seek more wheat this weekend - trade.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan may seek more wheat this weekend - trade.

text.p: Pakistan, facing flour shortages, may seek more wheat this weekend than many U.S. exporters had initially speculated, exporters said.

Several U.S. exporters had said on Wednesday that Pakistan might tender for anywhere from 200,000 to 300,000 tonnes of optional origin soft white wheat as early as this weekend, with the United States the most likely supplier.

Quantities now ranged from seven cargoes, totaling anywhere from 315,000 to 600,000 tonnes. "I would be more comfortable using the seven cargoes for May/June," one U.S. soft white wheat exporter said.
"Apparently Pakistan will make an announcement over the weekend about the tender," he said. "Offers are expected to go out by the middle of next week."

If the sale was set for May shipment, he said he believed the United States had a good chance of getting the business. But if shipment is for June, the Australian Wheat Board might take part of it, he said.

Another exporter agreed that the amount could be higher due to a flour shortage which has sparked unrest in several Pakistani cities. "Logistically, Pakistan can take up to 10 cargoes in a month," he said.
"There is always a possibility that the government could overshoot the runway, so to speak, and get more than they need. What is helpful is that wheat prices have dropped off their highs."
Chicago Board of Trade wheat futures tumbled in fast trade on Thursday on forecasts for rains in Europe and cool, wet weather in the U.S. hard red winter wheat growing regions, Chicago traders said.

Pakistani opposition leader Benazir Bhutto on April 20 called for an inquiry into a flour shortage that has sparked unrest in several cities. But the Pakistan Flour Mills Association said the flour crisis was almost over in the port city of Karachi, where fresh supplies had been trucked in from the interior.
Pakistan imported 1.8 million tonnes of wheat in July-March 1996/97 compared to 1.5 million in the year-ago period.
